name: body/max-lines
summary: The instructions stay short enough to be read rather than skimmed.
rationale: Past roughly five hundred lines an agent starts skimming. Progressive disclosure is the documented answer: an overview in SKILL.md, detail in files it references.
advice: Move the detail into files beside SKILL.md and reference them by path, keeping the body an overview that is read end to end.
reference_title: Skill authoring best practices — Claude Docs

name: body/no-secret
summary: The instructions carry no credential.
rationale: A skill is delivered into an agent's context and is often shared with a workspace. A secret in it is a secret in every session that fetches it.
advice: Take the credential out and rotate it: it has been in every session that fetched this, so removing it here is the second step, not the first.
reference_title: Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills — Anthropic Engineering

name: body/no-time-bomb
summary: No instruction is conditional on a date.
rationale: Anything conditional on a date is wrong on one side of it, and the agent has no way to tell which side it is on.
advice: Drop the date condition. If the old behaviour still matters, put it in an "Older versions" section rather than in a branch.
reference_title: Skill authoring best practices — Claude Docs

name: body/not-empty
summary: The instructions say something to do.
rationale: A heading with nothing under it delivers a heading. The body is the entire value of a skill once it has been selected.
advice: Write the steps. If the skill is a pointer to bundled files, say what to read and when.
reference_title: Agent Skills overview — Claude Docs

name: body/posix-paths
summary: Paths use forward slashes.
rationale: A backslash separator resolves nowhere except on Windows, including in the container the agent most likely unpacks the bundle into.
advice: Use forward slashes. Bundled paths are POSIX wherever the agent unpacks them.
reference_title: The AgentSkill specification

name: body/relative-paths
summary: Paths are relative to the skill rather than to a machine.
rationale: A path under /Users or ~ exists on the author's machine and nowhere else. Bundled files are addressed relative to the skill directory.
advice: Make the path relative to the skill directory, which is where the bundle is unpacked.
reference_title: The AgentSkill specification

name: body/token-budget
summary: The instructions fit the context they are loaded into.
rationale: A skill's body is loaded whole the moment it is selected, alongside the conversation, the tool schemas and everything else. The published guidance is to keep it under about five thousand tokens, and the median skill in the wild is a third of that.
advice: Move the detail into referenced files, which are loaded only when they are needed rather than on every activation.
reference_title: Skill authoring best practices — Claude Docs

name: bundle/contents-list
summary: A long reference file opens with a contents list.
rationale: An agent previewing a long file with a partial read cannot see what else is in it. A contents list at the top survives the preview.
advice: Add a contents list at the top, built from the headings already in the file.
reference_title: Skill authoring best practices — Claude Docs

name: bundle/declared-dependencies
summary: A script's third-party imports are ones the instructions say to install.
rationale: The agent runs the script, it fails on an import, and nothing in the instructions ever said what to install.
advice: Name the package and the install command in the instructions, at the step that runs the script.
reference_title: Skill authoring best practices — Claude Docs

name: bundle/executable-script
summary: A script with a shebang is marked executable.
rationale: It starts with a shebang, so it is meant to be run — and it arrives in the bundle without the bit set and fails on the first attempt.
advice: Set the executable bit, so the script arrives runnable.
reference_title: The AgentSkill specification

name: bundle/flat-references
summary: Bundled files are referenced from SKILL.md rather than from each other.
rationale: A file reached only through another file is often read in part or not at all. Progressive disclosure works one level deep.
advice: Reference the file from SKILL.md directly, so it hangs off the document the agent always reads.
reference_title: Skill authoring best practices — Claude Docs

name: bundle/no-dangling-path
summary: Every path the instructions name is in the bundle.
rationale: The instructions name a path the agent will not find after unpacking. This is the failure a diff cannot show and a linter can.
advice: Add the file to the bundle, or take the reference out of the instructions.
reference_title: The AgentSkill specification

name: bundle/unused-file
summary: Every bundled file is named by something.
rationale: A file nothing refers to is downloaded every time the bundle is materialised and read by nobody. It is a standing cost with no reader.
advice: Reference it from the instructions, or remove it from the bundle.
reference_title: Authoring Agent Skills: a software-engineering approach

name: description/concrete-noun
summary: The description names something a request would contain.
rationale: Matching happens on words. A skill about YouTube transcripts whose description never says YouTube cannot be matched on, however well it is written otherwise.
advice: Name the tools, formats or systems this is about — the nouns a request would use, not their categories.
reference_title: Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills — Anthropic Engineering

name: description/max-length
summary: The description is within the specification's 1024 characters.
rationale: The specification caps a description at 1024 characters because it is injected into a system prompt. Past the limit it is truncated wherever it happens to land, and the trigger clause is usually at the end.
advice: Cut it under 1024 characters. Lead with what it does and end with when to use it, so a truncation loses the least.
reference_title: The AgentSkill specification

name: description/min-length
summary: The description is long enough to route on.
rationale: An agent chooses between everything available on the strength of this sentence alone. A handful of words cannot carry both what the skill does and when to use it.
advice: Say what it does and when to use it — two clauses, around 150 to 300 characters, in the words a request would contain.
reference_title: Skill authoring best practices — Claude Docs

name: description/no-markup
summary: The description carries no tags.
rationale: The description is injected into a system prompt as text. A tag in it is read as content rather than as markup, and the specification forbids it.
advice: Remove the tags. The description is a sentence, not a document.
reference_title: The AgentSkill specification

name: description/not-just-name
summary: The description adds something the name does not already say.
rationale: The name is already in the agent's context. A description that restates it adds no signal to route on.
advice: Add what the name cannot say: the inputs it expects, the situation it fits, the words a user would type.
reference_title: Skill authoring best practices — Claude Docs

name: description/present
summary: The skill declares a description.
rationale: The description is the only thing an agent sees before it decides whether to fetch the skill. Without one there is nothing to route on, and the skill is effectively invisible.
advice: Add a description saying what the skill does and when to use it, in the words a request would contain.
reference_title: Skill authoring best practices — Claude Docs

name: description/says-when
summary: The description says when to use the skill.
rationale: Without a trigger clause the agent has to infer relevance from a summary. This is the single most common reason a skill is never selected.
advice: Append a trigger clause — "Use when …" followed by the situation, in the phrasing a request would actually use.
reference_title: Skill authoring best practices — Claude Docs

name: description/third-person
summary: The description is written in the third person.
rationale: It is injected into a system prompt, where a point of view that shifts between skills measurably hurts selection. "Processes Excel files", not "I can help you with Excel".
advice: Rewrite it in the third person: what the skill does, not what you or the agent will do for the reader.
reference_title: Skill authoring best practices — Claude Docs

name: frontmatter/key-format
summary: Metadata keys are addressable.
rationale: A key with a space in it, or one shadowing a defined field with different capitalisation, will not resolve the way its author expects wherever the skill is loaded.
advice: Rename the key without spaces, in lowercase, using hyphens between words.
reference_title: The AgentSkill specification

name: frontmatter/present
summary: The document opens with a frontmatter block.
rationale: Without frontmatter there is no declared name and no description, so nothing an agent selects on exists. The file is instructions nobody will ever be routed to.
advice: Open the file with a --- block declaring at least a name and a description.
reference_title: The AgentSkill specification

name: llm/consistent-terminology
summary: One word per concept, throughout.
rationale: The same thing called a field, a box and a control makes the agent work out that they are one thing before it can follow anything.
advice: Choose one word per concept and use it everywhere, including in the bundled files.
reference_title: Authoring Agent Skills: a software-engineering approach

name: llm/default-choice
summary: Where several approaches are offered, one is the default.
rationale: A list of equivalent approaches spends context and leaves the choice open at the moment the agent is least equipped to make it.
advice: Name a default and keep the rest as an escape hatch.
reference_title: Skill authoring best practices — Claude Docs

name: llm/failure-path
summary: A step that can fail says what to do when it does.
rationale: Without a recovery path the agent invents one, differently each time.
advice: Say what to do when that step fails — retry, fall back, or stop and report.
reference_title: Authoring Agent Skills: a software-engineering approach

name: llm/no-ambiguity
summary: No instruction can be read two ways, and none contradicts another.
rationale: Two readings means the agent will sometimes take the other one, and nothing in the run will say which it took.
advice: Pick one reading and delete the other.
reference_title: Authoring Agent Skills: a software-engineering approach

name: llm/no-known-context
summary: The instructions do not explain what the model already knows.
rationale: Context the model has anyway is a cost with no benefit, and it competes for attention with the part of the skill that is actually specific to you.
advice: Cut the paragraph. A capable model already has it, and what is left is what only you can say.
reference_title: Skill authoring best practices — Claude Docs

name: llm/output-example
summary: Where the output format matters, an example shows it.
rationale: An input and output pair conveys a format more reliably than a paragraph describing one.
advice: Add one worked example of the output, in the format the caller expects.
reference_title: Skill authoring best practices — Claude Docs

name: llm/specificity-matches-risk
summary: Detail matches how badly a step can go wrong.
rationale: An irreversible step described loosely invites improvisation; a judgement call pinned to an exact script stops the agent using what it can see.
advice: Match the detail to the risk: exact commands for what cannot be undone, direction and room for what is a judgement call.
reference_title: Skill authoring best practices — Claude Docs

name: llm/trigger-coverage
summary: The plausible phrasings of a request would route here.
rationale: The likely wordings of a request are written out and matched against this description. A phrasing that loses is a session where the skill never fires, and the user will not know to ask for it by name.
advice: Fold the phrasings that would not route into the description — the nouns a request would contain, and the situation it is asked in.
reference_title: Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills — Anthropic Engineering

name: name/format
summary: The name is lowercase, hyphenated, and at most 64 characters.
rationale: The name is an address as well as a label: it appears in a listing, in a fetch, and in a directory on disk. The specification restricts it to [a-z0-9-] so that all three agree.
advice: Rename it in lowercase with single hyphens between words, and keep it under 64 characters.
reference_title: The AgentSkill specification

name: name/matches-directory
summary: The declared name matches the directory the skill lives in.
rationale: The directory is what a bundle unpacks into and what most tooling addresses the skill by. When the two disagree, one of them is wrong wherever the skill is used next.
advice: Rename the directory, or the name in the frontmatter, so the two agree.
reference_title: Agent Skills overview — Claude Docs

name: name/no-reserved-word
summary: The name does not contain a reserved vendor word.
rationale: Names carrying a vendor's own word are reserved by the specification, and a skill using one can be refused on upload rather than at review.
advice: Take the vendor word out of the name. What the skill does is the part worth naming it after.
reference_title: The AgentSkill specification

name: name/not-generic
summary: The name says what the skill does.
rationale: A name like helper or utils tells an agent nothing and collides with the next one like it. The name is part of what a request is matched against.
advice: Rename it after what it does — the domain and the action, as in cull-photos rather than helper.
reference_title: Skill authoring best practices — Claude Docs

name: project/distinct-descriptions
summary: No two descriptions read as the same offer.
rationale: Two descriptions that overlap this much make selection a coin toss, and the loser looks like dead weight in any usage report.
advice: Differentiate them: name what each one covers that the other does not, in the first clause.
reference_title: Skill authoring best practices — Claude Docs

name: project/unique-name
summary: No two skills declare the same name.
rationale: The name is an address. Two skills sharing one means whichever is loaded second wins, and which one that is depends on the order a directory happened to be walked in.
advice: Rename one of them after what makes it different from the other.
reference_title: The AgentSkill specification
